label: Thursday, September 10
script:
There is a very particular kind of embarrassment that only happens when something enormous, armed, and confident gets absolutely wrecked by something small, feathered, or squishy. History is stuffed with it, and once you start looking you cannot stop finding it.

Start in the wheat country of Western Australia, November 1932. Farmers had spent a season watching flightless, six foot tall birds trample their crops into confetti, so the government sent actual soldiers, with actual Lewis machine guns, to solve the emu problem the way governments solve most problems. The emus had other plans. They scattered into small, fast moving squads the moment the shooting started, the guns jammed in the dust, and after several days and thousands of rounds spent, the operation was quietly abandoned. Newspapers at the time did not treat it as a joke, they treated it as a genuine military failure, because it was one. The emus went back to eating wheat. Nobody gave them a medal, but they earned one.

Fly forward exactly seventy five years and swap the desert for the actual vacuum of space. In 2007 the European Space Agency strapped a payload of tardigrades, water bears the size of a grain of sand, onto a satellite and launched them into orbit with no protection at all. No suit, no capsule, just raw exposure to solar radiation and the total emptiness that kills a human in about fifteen seconds. The tardigrades shriveled themselves into a dried out survival state called a tun, sat there for ten days getting cooked by cosmic rays, then came home, rehydrated, and started laying eggs like nothing had happened. Researchers led by Ingemar Jonsson published the results and casually confirmed that the toughest animal on Earth might also be the toughest animal off it.

Rewind now a full century further back, to a manicured hunting ground outside Paris in 1807. Napoleon, fresh off a military triumph, asked his chief of staff Berthier to arrange a nice relaxing rabbit hunt for the top brass. Berthier, wanting to guarantee a good show, ordered up several hundred rabbits rather than trusting the local wild population. The problem was the supplier delivered farm raised rabbits, tame ones, thoroughly used to seeing a human and expecting breakfast. The moment the cages opened, the rabbits did not scatter into the woods, they sprinted straight at the hunting party, climbed Napoleon's legs, and swarmed his carriage in a fluffy, hungry, unstoppable tide. The man who had rearranged the map of Europe was chased off a field by bunnies looking for lunch.

Now step inside the Louvre, August 1911. A museum handyman named Vincenzo Peruggia had spent his shifts working near a certain famous portrait behind glass, and one slow Monday he simply hid in a closet overnight, lifted the painting off the wall the next morning, tucked it under his coat, and walked out the staff entrance. The Mona Lisa was gone for two years, and its absence did more for its reputation than four centuries on the wall ever had. Newspapers ran the story daily, tourists lined up to stare at the empty hooks, and when the painting turned up in Florence, its return was treated like a celebrity homecoming. Before the theft, it was one respected portrait among many. After it, it was the most famous painting on the planet, thanks entirely to a guy with a coat and a bad plan.

Four different problems, four different centuries, and the same lesson refusing to sink in. Underestimate the small, the tame, the microscopic, or the overlooked, and it will eventually make a fool out of whatever thinks it is in charge. The emus, the water bears, the rabbits, and one stolen painting all somehow agree on that.

New file Monday, Wednesday, Saturday.

cases.q: In 1932, the Australian military was deployed with machine guns against an enemy that ultimately won. Who, or what, was the enemy?
cases.revealText: In November 1932, soldiers armed with Lewis machine guns were sent to cull emus destroying Western Australian wheat crops. The birds scattered too fast, the guns jammed in the dust, and after thousands of rounds fired the operation was called off. It is remembered as the Great Emu War, and the emus, functionally, won.
cases.source: The Argus, 1932 newspaper archives, and Australian War Memorial records

cases.q: Which tiny animal survived direct exposure to the vacuum and radiation of outer space during a 2007 European Space Agency experiment?
cases.revealText: Water bears, called tardigrades, were strapped to a satellite and launched into orbit, then exposed directly to the vacuum of space plus solar and cosmic radiation for ten days. Most survived by drying themselves into a near dead husk called a tun and later rehydrated normally. Published in Current Biology, 2008, led by researcher Ingemar Jonsson.

cases.q: In 1807, Napoleon organized a grand rabbit hunt that went disastrously wrong because the rabbits did what instead of fleeing?
options: Charged at Napoleon and his men
cases.revealText: Chief of staff Berthier supplied what he thought were wild rabbits, but they were actually farm raised bunnies used to being fed by humans. Once released, the mob mistook the hunting party for dinner and swarmed Napoleon's legs and carriage, forcing him to retreat.
cases.source: Memoirs of Baron Fain, cited in David Chandler's The Campaigns of Napoleon

cases.q: What event in 1911 turned the Mona Lisa from a respected painting into the most famous artwork in the world?
options: It was stolen from the Louvre
It was auctioned for a record price
It was damaged by an acid attack
cases.revealText: Louvre handyman Vincenzo Peruggia hid overnight in a closet, then walked out with the painting under his coat the next morning. It vanished for two years, made international headlines daily, and when it was recovered in Florence the frenzy had already cemented it as the most famous painting on Earth.
cases.source: Louvre official archives, and The Crimes of Paris by Dolnick

label: Saturday, September 12
script:
Picture London in July of 1858, when the Thames stopped being a river and started being a punishment. Decades of raw sewage had baked in the summer heat until the smell rolled off the water like a physical wall. Members of Parliament, sitting right on the riverbank, soaked their curtains in chloride of lime and still gagged through debates. Newspapers called it the Great Stink, which undersells it, because this was a smell so committed it basically wrote its own legislation. Within weeks the government fast tracked funding for engineer Joseph Bazalgette to build the sewer network that still runs under London today. Sometimes progress needs a push, and sometimes that push is several hundred tons of Victorian poop refusing to be ignored.

Around the same century, a very different kind of opening was teaching doctors what happens inside a human body. In 1822 a young fur trader named Alexis St Martin took a shotgun blast to the side at close range and, against all odds, survived. What he was left with was a hole into his own stomach that never fully sealed. Army surgeon William Beaumont saw an opportunity nobody had ever had before, a living window into digestion, and he took it, for over a decade, tying bits of food to string and lowering them into St Martin's stomach to watch what the body did with them. It sounds like something out of a fever dream, but it produced the first real science of gastric digestion, published in 1833, and it worked because one man's terrible injury became another man's laboratory.

Meanwhile, painters had their own uncomfortable secret sitting in tubes on their shelves. Mummy Brown was a rich, warm pigment beloved by artists for centuries, prized for glazing shadows and skin tones. The catch was in the name. It was made, quite literally, by grinding up embalmed Egyptian mummies, mixed with bitumen and resin to make a paste any painter could squeeze onto a palette. Pre Raphaelite painter Edward Burne Jones used it for years before finding out what was actually in it. Once he knew, he couldn't unknow it, so he marched into his garden and buried the tube with something close to a proper funeral, giving a stranger's remains the dignity his art supplies never had.

And then there's Marie Curie, who spent years handling radium and polonium with her bare hands, in an era before anyone understood what that would cost her. She died of the exposure, but her legacy kept glowing long after, quite literally. Her lab notebooks, her furniture, even a cookbook she used, still register on a Geiger counter more than a hundred years later. They're kept today in lead lined boxes at the National Library of France, and if you want to read Curie's own handwriting, you have to sign a waiver and put on protective gear first. Her genius outlived her, and so, strangely, did the danger.

What connects a stinking river, a hole in a man's side, a painter's guilty pigment and a radioactive notebook is the same very human habit, holding onto things that are too dangerous, too gross or too important to just throw away. We built cities on top of our worst smells, built science on top of a wound, built art on top of the dead, and built history on top of a woman's own body giving everything to understanding matter itself. Curiosity has never been polite, and it's rarely been clean, but it's always been how we learn. New file Monday, Wednesday, Saturday.

cases.q: In 1858, what finally convinced the British Parliament to fund a real sewer system for London?
options: The stench of raw sewage in the Thames baking in summer heat
A flood that destroyed the House of Commons library
cases.revealText: In summer 1858 the Thames stank so badly that Parliament soaked its curtains in chloride of lime and nearly abandoned the chamber. Engineer Joseph Bazalgette got emergency funding almost overnight to build the sewer system London still relies on today.

cases.q: What unusual injury let 19th century surgeon William Beaumont directly observe human digestion for the first time?
options: A gunshot wound that left a permanent opening into the stomach
cases.revealText: Fur trader Alexis St Martin survived a shotgun blast in 1822 that never fully sealed, leaving a direct window into his stomach. Beaumont spent over a decade lowering food on strings into the opening, founding the modern science of digestion.
cases.source: William Beaumont, Experiments and Observations on the Gastric Juice and the Physiology of Digestion, 1833

cases.q: What was the horrifying secret ingredient in the 19th century paint pigment called Mummy Brown?
cases.revealText: Mummy Brown really was made by grinding embalmed Egyptian mummies with resin and bitumen, and it was a staple pigment for painters including the Pre Raphaelites. When Edward Burne Jones learned what was in his paint tube, he buried it in his garden with a small funeral.
cases.source: Philip McCouat, The Life and Death of Mummy Brown, Journal of Art in Society

cases.q: Why do visitors have to sign a waiver and wear protective gear to read Marie Curie's personal notebooks today?
options: The notebooks are still radioactive over a century later
They are kept in a bank vault requiring insurance
cases.revealText: Marie Curie handled radium and polonium so extensively that her lab notebooks and even a personal cookbook remain radioactive today. They are stored in lead lined boxes at the National Library of France, and anyone wanting to see them must sign a liability waiver first.
cases.source: Bibliotheque nationale de France archival records, American Institute of Physics

label: Monday, September 14
script:
Every good disaster starts with somebody deciding a bad idea is actually a great one. Strasbourg, July 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea steps into the street and starts dancing. Not fun dancing. Not wedding dancing. The kind of dancing where your feet bleed through your shoes and you keep going anyway. Within days the neighbors join her, not because it looks fun but because whatever this is, it spreads. City records put the number past a hundred, some accounts push it toward four hundred, all of them jerking and spinning in the summer heat while officials scratched their heads. The town physicians diagnosed hot blood and prescribed the exact wrong cure, more dancing, hired musicians, a stage, the works. People reportedly dropped dead from strokes and exhaustion mid step while a paid band kept the rhythm going. Nobody hit the brakes because nobody understood there were brakes to hit.

Fast forward to 1970, coastal Oregon, and a sperm whale the size of a school bus washes up dead and rotting on the beach at Florence. The Oregon Highway Division, tasked with cleanup, decides the fix is dynamite, half a ton of it, packed against the carcass with the cheerful logic that scavenger birds would happily eat the smaller pieces left behind. A crowd gathers to watch. The blast goes off and instead of tidy whale confetti, chunks of blubber the size of couches rain from the sky, one of them crushing a car parked a quarter mile away. The birds, it turns out, never got their snack, they fled the second the fuse was lit. Nobody died, which honestly feels like a technicality.

Around the same era on the other side of the timeline, in 1606, a much more deliberate kind of chaos was unfolding in Rome. Caravaggio, the most talented and least stable painter of his generation, kills a man named Ranuccio Tomassoni in a street fight, possibly over a bet, possibly over a woman, nobody fully agrees. With a death sentence hanging over him he runs, first to Naples, then Malta, then Sicily, painting some of the most violent, shadow drenched masterpieces in Western art while actively being a wanted man. The brushwork gets darker as the manhunt tightens. He dies at 38 under circumstances still argued about today, a genius who never once considered that maybe running from your problems and also being extremely famous were not compatible strategies.

And then there is Thomas Hicks, marathon runner, 1904 Olympics, St Louis, in brutal heat with dust roads and almost no water stations because organizers thought dehydration built character. Hicks starts fading around mile twenty, so his handlers do what any responsible team would do, they inject him with strychnine sulfate and hand him a shot of brandy. Twice. Strychnine, a rat poison, in small doses acts as a stimulant, and at the time there were no rules against it because nobody had thought to write any. Hicks crosses the finish line hallucinating, barely conscious, needing two men to hold him upright, and still wins gold.

Four different centuries, four different kinds of people convinced that going further was always the answer, more dancing, more dynamite, more running, more risk. Sometimes the body keeps its own accounting no matter what the crowd or the officials or the trainers believe, and sometimes it takes a whale exploding over a parking lot to prove the point. New file Monday, Wednesday, Saturday.

cases.q: In July 1518, what happened to hundreds of people in Strasbourg that physicians blamed on hot blood?
options: They danced uncontrollably for days, some until they died
cases.revealText: In July 1518 a woman named Frau Troffea started dancing in a Strasbourg street and could not stop. Within weeks city records counted well over a hundred people doing the same, some collapsing from exhaustion or stroke. Physicians prescribed more dancing as the cure, which made everything worse.
cases.source: John Waller, A Time to Dance, a Time to Die

cases.q: In 1970, Oregon highway engineers tried to dispose of a beached whale using which method that went spectacularly wrong?
options: Towing it back out to sea
cases.revealText: When a dead sperm whale washed ashore at Florence, Oregon, officials packed it with dynamite expecting scavenger sized pieces to remain. Instead huge chunks of blubber rained on the crowd and crushed a parked car a quarter mile away. Nobody died, but the footage became legendary long before anything went viral.

cases.q: Which Baroque painter killed a man in a Rome street brawl in 1606 and spent his final years as a fugitive?
cases.revealText: Caravaggio killed Ranuccio Tomassoni in a 1606 brawl and fled Rome with a death sentence over his head. He kept producing violent, shadow heavy masterpieces while on the run through Naples, Malta, and Sicily. He died at 38, still wanted, under circumstances nobody has fully settled.
cases.source: Andrew Graham-Dixon, Caravaggio, A Life Sacred and Profane

cases.q: What substance combo helped Thomas Hicks win the 1904 Olympic marathon despite nearly collapsing from it?
cases.revealText: Thomas Hicks was dosed twice with strychnine sulfate and brandy by his handlers during the brutal 1904 St Louis marathon, a legal move since anti doping rules did not exist yet. He crossed the finish line hallucinating and unable to stand on his own. He still took home the gold.
cases.source: David Davis, Showdown at Shepherd's Bush

label: Wednesday, September 16
script:
Every good disaster starts the same way, something gets bottled up until it can't be anymore. Boston, January 1919, the North End is stacked with tenements and a steel tank fifty feet tall, holding two point three million gallons of molasses meant for munitions and rum. It's an unseasonably warm afternoon and the tank has been groaning for years, rivets popping, kids swiping drips of molasses through the seams for a free snack. Then it just lets go. A wave taller than a two story house tears down Commercial Street at highway speed, ripping buildings off their foundations, drowning horses standing up, killing twenty one people in a flood that moves too fast to outrun and too thick to swim in. Cleanup crews used salt water and sand for months, and old timers swore for decades after that on a hot day, you could still smell it in the harbor.

Antarctica keeps its pressure differently, in the dark, for a lot longer. Under Taylor Glacier there's a pocket of brine that's been sealed away for more than a million years, so salty it stays liquid inside solid ice, so iron rich it looks like tomato soup. When it finally finds a crack and dribbles out onto the glacier's face, the iron meets oxygen for the first time in a million years and rusts on contact, right there in the open air, staining the ice a horror movie red. Explorers found it in 1911 and had no idea what they were looking at. It took until 2017 and a team dragging radar equipment across the ice to actually trace the buried plumbing and prove the water had been down there since before humans existed.

Something similar, weirdly, happens inside a jellyfish smaller than your fingernail. Turritopsis dohrnii gets old, gets hurt, gets stressed by starvation or a change in water temperature, and instead of dying like a normal animal, its adult cells start walking backward. Muscle cells turn into nerve cells, tentacles retract, the whole creature collapses down into the blob shaped polyp stage it started life as, a biological reset button most animals don't get to press twice. It's not immortality exactly, plenty die to predators or bad luck, but the aging clock itself just refuses to stay wound forward. Scientists have watched it happen under a microscope, over and over, since the early nineties, and nobody has fully cracked how the cells know the way back.

Michelangelo held his pressure a different way, on purpose, in fresco. Painting The Last Judgment on the Sistine Chapel wall in his sixties, he got an earful from Biagio da Cesena, the pope's master of ceremonies, who thought all that nudity belonged in a tavern, not a chapel. Michelangelo said nothing, kept painting, and quietly slipped Biagio into the scene as Minos, judge of the underworld, complete with donkey ears and a snake sinking its teeth into his crotch. Biagio complained to the pope. The pope reportedly said his jurisdiction didn't extend to hell, so the portrait stayed, and five hundred years later tourists still walk past a Renaissance grudge painted directly onto the ceiling of one of the holiest rooms on earth.

A tank, a glacier, a jellyfish, a fresco, none of them built to hold what they were holding forever. Molasses breaks its rivets, brine finds its crack, a jellyfish rewinds its own clock, and one insulted painter turns a complaint into eternal punishment. Pressure always finds a way out, it just picks its moment. New file Monday, Wednesday, Saturday.

cases.q: What sticky disaster tore through Boston's North End in January 1919, killing 21 people?
options: A burst tank unleashing a giant wave of molasses
A runaway train full of maple syrup
An explosion at a candy factory
cases.revealText: A two point three million gallon molasses storage tank burst on Commercial Street, sending a wave reportedly moving around 35 miles per hour through the neighborhood. It killed 21 people and injured about 150, and cleanup took months with sand and salt water.
cases.source: Smithsonian Magazine, coverage of the Great Molasses Flood of 1919

cases.q: Which tiny sea creature can reverse its own aging by turning its adult cells back into an earlier baby stage?
cases.revealText: When stressed, injured, or starving, Turritopsis dohrnii can undergo transdifferentiation, converting mature cells back into the polyp stage it began life as, essentially resetting its biological clock. Researchers have observed the process repeatedly under lab conditions since the 1990s.
cases.source: Scientific American, "Can a Jellyfish Unlock the Secret of Immortality"

cases.q: Which Renaissance artist took revenge on a papal critic by painting him into hell with donkey ears and a snake biting his crotch?
cases.revealText: In The Last Judgment on the Sistine Chapel wall, Michelangelo painted Vatican official Biagio da Cesena as Minos, judge of the underworld, after Biagio complained the fresco's nudity was obscene. The insult stayed on the wall, reportedly because the pope joked his authority did not reach into hell.
cases.source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists

cases.q: What causes Antarctica's Blood Falls to ooze bright red liquid out of a glacier?
options: Iron rich ancient brine that rusts the instant it hits air
cases.revealText: Blood Falls is fed by salty, iron rich brine trapped beneath Taylor Glacier for over a million years, staying liquid because of its salt content even inside the ice. When it seeps out and meets oxygen, the iron rusts instantly, dyeing the ice red, a mystery first noted in 1911 and mapped with radar in a 2017 study.
cases.source: Journal of Glaciology, Mikucki et al., with National Geographic coverage
